title: With busy Thanksgiving travel ahead, how likely are disruptions? | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

More than a million people were stranded at airports across the country on Friday after the agency in charge of transporting passengers safely had toground all planes— just two weeks before the start of the busiest travel season of the year.

For just the second time since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded aircraft nationwide. The notice stated it was due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

During a news conference over the weekend, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that in at least one remote FAA location, contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from anold copper wire to modern fiber optics.

At this point, he said, it’s unclear whether contractor error or faulty equipment during the switch caused the meltdown. The FAA will investigate the cause of the issue.

The FBI is examining the router and other equipment behind the meltdown, according to a person familiar with the investigation. The plan is to try to reconstruct what happened and replicate the technical issue the FAA says overloaded the system and caused it to have gaps in communications, the person said.

The FBI is assisting FAA and L3Harris in examining the equipment, an FBI spokesman said on X.

CNN previously reported that there was no immediate indication of a security threat or nefarious attack behind the nationwide FAA flight ground stop.

A senior administration official told CNN that an FAA communications facility at South Arkansas Regional Airport in El Dorado, Arkansas, was the site of telecommunications work underway on Friday before the nationwide ground stop.

The airport is home to a Remote Communications Outlet, or RCO, a small radio installation that allows pilots to communicate with flight service personnel located elsewhere. The FAA also lists other remote aviation communications equipment in El Dorado. It is not yet clear which specific installation was involved in Friday’s work.

The agency has been replacing the country’s dated copper wiring of the antiquated air traffic control system, in dire need of an upgrade that has bipartisan support to complete, sinceat least 2025when the DOT announced its plans to modernize the whole system. However, this project has remained a source of frustration for Democrats and Republicans alike, as several administrations have come and gone and the modernization work has not been completed for varying reasons.

“We have to make the transition,” Duffy told reporters on Saturday morning. “We’re making the transition not because we want to spend money. We’re making the transition because it’s safer and it’s more resilient.”

This massive disruption, which cascaded in the days after as airlines attempted to reposition crews and planes to get passengers where they needed to go, comes just ahead of the massive Thanksgiving travel season. The Transportation Security Administration said it expects to screen potentially more than 3 million passengers nationwide.

Aviation officials didn’t seem confident that this kind of disruption won’t happen again, instead deflecting to the need for modernization and Duffy upping his ask to Congress for $50 billion to complete the work. Previously, he said he would need $30 billion.

“You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can’t wait for that,” Duffy said in response to a question from CNN’s Kristen Holmes on Friday.

With no quick or easy fix for a plagued system, travelers will need to be mindful as they make plans for the holidays.

At the start of the airspace meltdown, two places were “pinging” the FAA’s network at a “very high rate” of 1,000 connections over every four to five seconds, according to Rebecca Guy, FAA acting chief technology officer.

“We disabled both of those right away, and we’re able to stabilize our network,” Guy told reporters. “That router that we think was the original, we stopped functionality and all of that across the (National Airspace System.)”

As a precaution,the FAA also disabledapproximately 60 similar routers in the system.

“At this time, we do believe what occurred with that router has been worked through,” she said.

One reporter asked whether the FAA knew one faulty router had the capability to have such a massive impact on the system.

“We did not,” Guy replied. “That is exactly why we want to continue to verify and do analysis as we go forward.”

The solution Duffy, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford and Guy emphasized during the ground stop and the days after is more money to modernize the system. Dave Riley, who worked as an air traffic controller for more than 30 years, said he wasn’t left feeling like the FAA had a real solution yet.

“I would like to think going forward that they’ll take many more precautions on how they do this type of work,” Riley told CNN.

Katie Thomson was the former deputy administrator of the FAA during the Biden administration. She said in this particular case, the FAA needs to be transparent.

“(The FAA) need(s) to be very careful about what they say,” Thomson told CNN. “They need to provide accurate information, and they need to also acknowledge what they don’t know, and try to provide some answers about when they think they will. And right now, I don’t think they provided sufficient level of information, and I will attribute it to the fact that they likely don’t know exactly what happened.”

She added, “It is highly unusual that switching out a router would take down an entire system,” but she credits the FAA for making decisions that are in the best interest of safety, like shutting down the airspace.

While many questions remain, the FAA and DOT believe they have made strides toupgrade the system,but there’s more work to be done.

The day after the ground stop, Duffy and officials touted what has been completed so far after the FAA received $12.5 billion from President Donald Trump’s spending bill last year. The money is on track to be spent by the end of 2028.

According to Duffy, the FAA has replaced 69% of copper communication lines to high-speed fiber, deployed surface awareness initiative technology at 143 control towers, converted 469 radio sites, installed electronic flight strips at 25 towers, installed 224 IP voice switch systems at towers, installed 18 new tower simulator systems, and installed nine SMR4 surface movement radars.

But more money from Congress is needed to complete the necessary overhaul, a project that Duffy has pushed for since May 2025.

“I hope that (Congress) meet(s) this moment, and they invest in what will be the state of the art, the best in class, best in the world air traffic control system,” Duffy said.

The secretary has also placed some blame on L3Harris for these problems, stating hewants to cut the contractorthat owns the nation’s leading air traffic surveillance network out of the agency’s modernization plan.

“These issues don’t happen, which begs the question for us: What did L3 Harris do? Did they make mistakes yesterday?” he said.

L3Harrishas said it is supportingthe FAA in its investigation.

Government watchdogs have issued their own warnings on the state of the new system.

In a Government Accountability Officereport from September,the findings state the FAA “has not developed a comprehensive and well-documented lifecycle cost estimate” for the brand-new air traffic control system.

“FAA has 11,389 individual project schedules that are not integrated,” the report states. “As a result, individual projects are scheduled for installations at the same sites, generally without optimizing the schedules to reduce impacts to controller operations. Officials stated they have plans to address this issue, however; they did not have a time frame for when the issue would be resolved.”

Duffy dismissed concerns that Friday’s system failure would impact travelers during the busy holiday season.

“My kids are flying next Friday back from college,” Duffy told reporters after the FAA called off the ground stop on Friday. “I think we’re going to be back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel during Thanksgiving.”

Bedford said after speaking with airline partners that operations would “be able to have full schedule integrity by the close of business on Sunday.”

Bedford and Duffy have both assured passengers that the system remains safe.

“Everything should proceed normally, normal operations,” Riley said. “I’m pretty confident about that. But the finer details of the impacts of this, I think, will last at least a week. So, I think it will be good by Thanksgiving.”

Thomson said if similar disruptions were to to happen over the Thanksgiving or Christmas holidays, it could have a very significant impact.

“It has national security implications,” Thomson said. “It obviously has economic implications when the system is shut down, and obviously implications for people who are trying to travel for business and to see family.”

Clint Henderson, managing editor at The Points Guy, told CNN passengers don’t have many rights in situations like these, but there are some things that they can do.

“If they cancel your flight and you decide not to travel, which may be a good bet in these kind of circumstances, you are entitled to a full refund,” Henderson said.

He added that passengers should keep their receipts for expenses incurred so the airlines, or even the government, could compensate. Travelers who booked with a credit card may have certain protections as well.

Delays and cancellations have gone down in the days after the ground stop, moving more travelers to where they need to be. TSA said the Sunday following Thanksgiving was TSA’s busiest day on record last year, when the agency screened more than 3.13 million passengers.

This year should be no different.

This story was updated to reflect that the FBI is examining the equipment as they assist the FAA and contractor L3Harris in examining the equipment.

CNN’s Pete Muntean and Evan Perez contributed to this report.

CNN’s Pete Muntean and Evan Perez contributed to this report.
